Herein
heer-IN
adv.
From here and in: in this thing, in this respect. Webster 1828: in this. John uses it as a pointer, and where he points is the definition of love, the ground of assurance, and the glory of the Father.

Biblical Definition

John’s herein is one of the great pointing words of the New Testament. It appears where he means to fix the reader’s eye on a definition and not let it drift: Herein is love, not that we loved God, but that he loved us, and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins (1 John 4:10). The sentence defines love by an act, and by an act whose direction is from God to man; the negative clause — not that we loved God — is there to prevent the reader from starting anywhere else. Three verses later he uses it again for assurance, and the ground is startling: Herein is our love made perfect, that we may have boldness in the day of judgment: because as he is, so are we in this world (1 John 4:17). Our Lord uses the same construction for the Father’s glory and makes fruitfulness the evidence of discipleship: Herein is my Father glorified, that ye bear much fruit; so shall ye be my disciples (John 15:8). Paul uses it of settled practice under examination: herein do I exercise myself, to have always a conscience void of offence toward God, and toward men (Acts 24:16).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines HEREIN as in this — that is, in this thing, matter, respect, or particular.

expand to see more

HEREIN, adv. — In this.

In this thing, matter, or particular; as, herein is our comfort.

Used to point emphatically at what immediately follows.

Compare HEREBY, by this; HEREOF, of this; HEREUPON, upon this.

From here and in; Anglo-Saxon her and in.

Key Scripture

1 John 4:10 — "Herein is love, not that we loved God, but that he loved us, and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins."

1 John 4:17 — "Herein is our love made perfect, that we may have boldness in the day of judgment: because as he is, so are we in this world."

John 15:8 — "Herein is my Father glorified, that ye bear much fruit; so shall ye be my disciples."

Acts 24:16 — "And herein do I exercise myself, to have always a conscience void of offence toward God, and toward men."

Modern Corruption

1 John 4:10 defines love by propitiation, and every account of the atonement that removes the appeasing of God’s wrath removes the very thing John points at when he says herein.

expand to see more

Herein is love — and the thing pointed at is a propitiation. The Greek word hilasmos means the turning away of wrath, and it is the word John chooses to define love with. This is the exact point at which much modern atonement theology departs. The moral-influence theory (Abelard, revived by liberal Protestantism) makes the cross a demonstration that moves us; the governmental theory makes it a display upholding God’s rule; more recent popular writing has gone further and called penal substitution unworthy of God. Each of these must first empty the word John uses. But Scripture says God set forth His Son as a propitiation through faith in His blood (Romans 3:25), and it says so in order to declare God righteous in justifying the ungodly. Remove the propitiation and the love has nothing to consist of, since it is defined here by no other content.

1 John 4:17 grounds boldness in the day of judgment on something outside the believer: as he is, so are we in this world. The assurance is not a measurement of the Christian’s progress but a statement of his standing in Christ — which is why the verse can speak of love made perfect and boldness in judgment in the same breath without contradiction. The Reformed doctrine of justification by imputed righteousness is what makes such a sentence sayable. If a believer’s acceptance rested on his sanctification, boldness in the day of judgment would be presumption; resting on Christ’s obedience reckoned to him, it is simple faith. John 15:8 then keeps the balance: much fruit is the evidence of discipleship, never its ground.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek en touto, in this — the phrase rendered herein; hilasmos (G2434), propitiation; parresia (G3954), boldness or freedom of speech.

expand to see more

Greek en touto — literally in this; John’s pointing phrase, rendered herein and hereby throughout his epistle.

Greek hilasmos (G2434) — propitiation, the turning away of wrath; the content of love in 1 John 4:10.

Greek parresia (G3954) — boldness, confidence, freedom of speech; boldness in the day of judgment (1 John 4:17).

Greek teleioo (G5048) — to bring to completeness; our love made perfect (1 John 4:17).

Greek askeo (G778) — to exercise oneself, to take pains; Paul’s word for his settled practice (Acts 24:16).

Usage

"Herein is love, not that we loved God, but that he loved us (1 John 4:10) — the negative clause prevents the reader starting anywhere else."

"Herein is our love made perfect, that we may have boldness in the day of judgment (1 John 4:17) — the ground is outside the believer."

"Herein is my Father glorified, that ye bear much fruit (John 15:8) — fruit is the evidence of discipleship, never its ground."
